prize_parts.citation: for the invention of the optical lattice clock, trapping neutral atoms at a magic wavelength so that the lattice does not perturb the clock transition, and for its development into frequency standards with uncertainties near one part in 10^18

statement.case_for: I keep the optical lattice clock as my preferred single part, and I want to be plain that this is a weighing of criteria and not a claim that the graphene case is weak. The chair asks what new physics, and not only new accuracy, lattice clocks have given. My answer is the following. Magic-wavelength trapping is a specific idea that turned a many-atom sample into a usable frequency reference, and it made clocks a probe of effects that were not accessible before: gravitational redshift resolved over millimetre-to-centimetre height differences within a single sample, density- and interaction-related shifts that required a many-body treatment of the clock ensemble, and comparisons between independent laboratories that bound variations of constants and violations of local position invariance at a level that earlier standards could not reach. I describe these from my general knowledge of the field and have not checked individual numbers against the supplied files. What I can say with confidence from my own area is that the relativistic atomic structure needed to understand the systematic shifts is well controlled, which is part of why the result is firm. The attribution is the cleanest on the shortlist: an idea and first demonstration by Katori, and the realisation of the accuracy and stability frontier by Ye's group, so two names fit the prize without arbitrary exclusion. Twenty years of independent confirmation across national laboratories means that neither the measurement nor its interpretation is in dispute. The citation I now propose says explicitly that the achievement is the lattice with a magic wavelength, which separates it from single-ion clocks and from the 2005 and 2012 prizes as Kroll asked. I treat a future redefinition of the second as a consequence that supports relevance but not as evidence of merit that the committee should count before it happens.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that six of eight round-1 files prefer magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene with an identical three-name set, and I rank it second. I do not dispute the prediction-then-discovery structure, the reproduction by many laboratories, or the originality of a single tuning parameter. If the committee's primary criterion is the opening of a new field by a confirmed prediction, B038 is the stronger case and I would be satisfied to see it awarded. Against my own preference: the discovery-versus-invention question is a real judgement call, and Olsson and Danielsson are right that the clock case is closer to a measurement capability than to the discovery of a new phase of matter. The 2005 and 2012 prizes make a third precision-metrology prize in two decades a fair objection. Credit is also incomplete: other lattice-clock groups, and the single-ion optical clock groups that reach comparable uncertainties, are outside the two names, and I have not verified every priority detail from the supplied text.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers B038 because one tunable parameter, the twist angle, controls bandwidth and interaction strength, and treats the unsettled pairing mechanism as something that recognition need not wait for.
responses.response: I accept the conceptual point about a single control parameter and I accept that the core observation is secure whether or not the mechanism is settled. Taking the chair's question to the B038 supporters, I would also say that a citation anchored on the prediction and the observed states survives a conventional pairing outcome, so my concern is narrower than mechanism. It is how fast the phase diagram is changing, with fractional Chern states and competing accounts of the superconducting state still emerging, which makes eight years short next to the twenty years of confirmation behind the clock. I weigh that as a difference of degree. It is why I keep B045 first but would not call a B038 prize premature.

responses.point: Olsson ranks B038 first as a clean discovery with a quantitative prediction, argues that sample and twist-angle disorder questions are understood from a materials side, and asks what new physics, as opposed to new accuracy, the lattice clocks have revealed.
responses.response: The question is fair and I have tried to answer it in my case: resolved gravitational redshift inside one sample, many-body shifts that forced the clock community to treat the ensemble quantum mechanically, and cross-laboratory comparisons that tighten bounds on varying constants. I will concede that it is new physics reached through accuracy and not a new phase, and that you may weigh that differently. On your materials point I am reassured about reproducibility, but device-to-device variation from twist-angle disorder still makes quantitative laboratory-to-laboratory comparison less direct than a clock comparison where the same transition is measured to 18 digits. That is a difference in how firm the numbers are, not in how interesting the physics is.

responses.point: Kroll also prefers B045 as a mature, independently confirmed advance, acknowledges the 2005 and 2012 prizes as an objection, notes that ion clocks reach similar uncertainties so the citation should say what is specific to lattices, and discloses a research stay in Hall's laboratory.
responses.response: I agree with the citation point and have rewritten mine to name the magic-wavelength lattice explicitly as the specific achievement. I disagree with nothing in the science of your case, but I want the committee to see that we are not independent supporters in the way the count suggests: your disclosed link to the JILA-adjacent environment bears on Ye, while I have no documented connection to Katori or Ye, and my relativistic atomic-structure expertise is only adjacent. If the committee decides that a disclosure of that kind should reduce the weight of B045 support, it should count mine and yours separately and not treat the two as a bloc. I also note your fallback of B007 and think it is a reasonable second choice among the quantum-technology entries, though I rank B001 and B038 above it.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks B038 first as a theory prediction matched by nature, ranks the clock fourth because it may overlap earlier metrology prizes, and says the attribution doubts about earlier twisted-graphene theory and the first author are as real as those he accepts for clocks.
responses.response: I take the symmetry point: attribution in B038 is contested at the edges in the same way as in B045 (Lopes dos Santos, Peres, Castro Neto and Yuan Cao on one side, the other lattice-clock and single-ion groups on the other). The difference I still see is in degree. In B045 the two names correspond to a clean idea-plus-realisation split that every member who ranked it has accepted, while in B038 several members including the proponents flag the exclusions as a source of controversy. On overlap with earlier prizes, I accept the objection is real and have not tried to argue it away. I think the lattice with a magic wavelength is a distinct achievement, but I cannot prove that to a colleague who sees metrology as one family.

responses.point: Pearce, the chair, moved from IceCube to B038 on the breadth of support, records no specific conflict on B038 or B045, and describes the maturity of interpretation as the main reservation about B038.
responses.response: I appreciate that you moved on the scientific arguments and not on the count, and I would rather the committee not treat six supporters as a substitute for scientific judgment either, in my favour or against it. On your question of whether the committee should accept the three-name set with no mechanism claimed, my answer is yes: a citation on the 2011 flat-band prediction and the 2018 observation of correlated and superconducting states is defensible, and the omissions are real but not disqualifying. The remaining question is only whether the field's age should weigh against it, and I have said where I come out on that.

responses.point: Eriksson moved DMFT to an alternative and now backs B038, noting that the credit is the weak point (Cao, Fatemi, earlier twisted-graphene theory) and that the wording of the citation should carry the uncertainty about mechanism.
responses.response: I agree that the credit problem is a question of citation wording, and that the right response to an unsettled mechanism is a citation that claims no mechanism. That is the same standard I apply to B045, where the citation should claim only what is specific to the lattice. Where we differ is on whether the omitted names tilt the decision. For me the cleaner two-name split in B045 counts as a real advantage, but I would not call the B038 credit indefensible.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards a precision-measurement advance as a discovery or as an instrument, and whether the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes make a lattice-clock prize look derivative.

Whether the specific new-physics results I cite for lattice clocks (resolved redshift within a sample, many-body clock shifts, bounds on varying constants) are stated at the right level of detail, since I have not verified them against the supplied files.
Whether other lattice-clock groups and single-ion optical clock groups should appear in the citation or in the credited names, because I have not verified the priority details.
Whether the age of B038 and the pace of change in its phase diagram should weigh against it relative to the maturity of B045, which is a weighting I hold with modest confidence.
Whether a redefinition of the second will occur on a timescale that matters; I treat it as relevance and not as merit.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my provided profile for B045, Katori or Ye, and none for B038 or its credited names. My documented collaborations (Anne L'Huillier, Ursula Keller's group, the Lund attosecond group, Schuch, Dahlstrom, Argenti, Indelicato) concern attosecond photoionisation and highly charged ions and do not involve any shortlisted candidate or credited person. My expertise in relativistic atomic structure is adjacent to atomic-clock physics, which I disclose as background and not as a personal connection. I note Kroll's disclosure about Ye's environment separately from my own position.
